design_detail: Narrative clinical review in NEJM's Review Article series, by a single author, on recognizing and managing alcohol withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens): mechanism and course of withdrawal, the DSM-5 criteria, prevalence, case fatality, predictors and treatment, with three tables (the CIWA-Ar scale, the DSM-5 criteria and a suggested treatment protocol) and 33 references. No search strategy, dates or inclusion criteria are stated, beyond a mention of a PubMed search for uncontrolled studies after a 2004 guideline; there is no quantitative synthesis.
can_establish: What one clinician-researcher, drawing on DSM-5, a 2004 evidence-based guideline and selected later studies, presented in 2014 as the recognition, course, risk factors and recommended management of alcohol withdrawal delirium, and how weak he judged the treatment evidence to be.
cannot_establish: The incidence, case fatality or predictors of withdrawal delirium (all figures are second-hand, given without the designs, settings or periods of their sources), the comparative effectiveness or safety of any drug or route (no trial is appraised), or the completeness of the evidence (no systematic search).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). 33 references chosen by the author: DSM-5; reviews and guidelines, including the 2004 guideline on withdrawal delirium (Mayo-Smith et al.), Cochrane reviews of benzodiazepines (Amato et al., 2010) and of magnesium (Sarai et al., 2013) for alcohol withdrawal, and the Royal College of Physicians guidance on Wernicke's encephalopathy; and primary studies of predictors and of individual drugs, some of them retrospective by their titles (refs 13 and 16) (references, p. 2113).
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the author's own. The treatment evidence named as the best is old (nine controlled trials conducted from 1959 to 1978, summarized in a 2004 guideline); later evidence is from uncontrolled studies found in a PubMed search whose terms and dates are not given (p. 2111); the prevalence, case-fatality and predictor figures come from cited studies whose settings and designs are not described (p. 2110). Three of the 33 references are the author's own.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable as an exposure study. The condition reviewed is alcohol withdrawal and withdrawal delirium after stopping or reducing heavy, prolonged drinking (DSM-5, Table 2, p. 2111); the drinking that precedes withdrawal is not quantified.
exposure.polysubstance: Recent misuse of other depressant drugs (the review's term) is named as a predictor of withdrawal delirium (p. 2110); other drug use is not otherwise discussed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Withdrawal symptoms are described as beginning within 8 hours of falling blood alcohol, peaking at about 72 hours and markedly reduced by days 5 to 7 (p. 2109); delirium as beginning about 3 days after withdrawal symptoms appear (p. 2110).

outcomes.instruments: Described, not applied: the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment of Alcohol Scale, revised (CIWA-Ar; 10 clinician-rated items, total 0 to 67) for withdrawal severity (Table 1, p. 2110), and the DSM-5 criteria for alcohol withdrawal and for delirium (Table 2, p. 2111).
outcomes.operationalization: Withdrawal delirium is DSM-5 alcohol withdrawal together with delirium (Table 2 footnote, p. 2111); withdrawal severity is banded by CIWA-Ar total score (Table 1 footnote, p. 2110).

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed. Descriptive figures as cited: lifetime alcohol use disorder in 20% of men and 10% of women in most Western societies; withdrawal symptoms in about 50% of people with an alcohol use disorder who cut down or stop, with seizures, delirium or both in 3 to 5% of them (p. 2109); withdrawal delirium in 3 to 5% of patients hospitalized for alcohol withdrawal; case fatality about 1 to 4% of hospitalized patients with withdrawal delirium; recent withdrawal seizures in 20% of people with delirium (p. 2110). No relative risks or intervals are given for any predictor.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. The studies of alternatives to benzodiazepines are cited for the amounts given, not for their results; harms are named for the alternative and adjunctive drugs but not for high-dose benzodiazepines; the PubMed search mentioned is not described (pp. 2111–2112).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The review is a clinical synthesis. Its descriptive figures (3 to 5% of patients hospitalized for withdrawal develop withdrawal delirium; about 1 to 4% of those die; onset about 3 days after withdrawal begins; duration usually 2 or 3 days) and its predictors are second-hand from cited studies, and its treatment advice rests, by its own account, on nine controlled trials from 1959 to 1978 summarized in a 2004 guideline and on later uncontrolled studies; no benzodiazepine has been shown superior to another, and the alternatives are less studied.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say withdrawal delirium is "best treated with intravenous benzodiazepines" (p. 2112), while also stating that all doses in the review are approximations based on uncontrolled studies and that data on the most effective care are lacking. Gaps: (1) the body cites no evidence comparing intravenous with other routes, or benzodiazepines with other drug classes, in withdrawal delirium; the preference rests on the 2004 guideline and clinical reviews; (2) Table 3 presents its regimens as suggested treatment without grading the evidence for each element, although the Conclusions concede they rest on uncontrolled data; (3) the statement that case fatality could be reduced by timely diagnosis and adequate treatment comes without data on the size of the reduction (p. 2110); (4) the dangers of the alternative and adjunctive drugs are named (heart block, QT prolongation, seizures) but the harms of the high benzodiazepine amounts the review describes are not, beyond recommending hospital or intensive care and vital-sign monitoring (pp. 2111–2112). The explanation offered for the lack of trials (low prevalence, cost, no profit motive) is hedged as a possibility. Because the review is candid about the weakness of the evidence, the gap is minor.

timeline.event: Schuckit et al. (1995), Addiction: histories of withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens in 1648 people with alcohol dependence; the author's own study, cited among the sources of the predictor list (ref. 17).

Mayo-Smith (1997), JAMA meta-analysis and evidence-based practice guideline on the pharmacological management of alcohol withdrawal (on the project's Tier A list); not cited in this review, which relies on the same first author's 2004 guideline on withdrawal delirium.

Mayo-Smith et al. (2004), Archives of Internal Medicine: evidence-based practice guideline on managing alcohol withdrawal delirium (ref. 9; on the project's Tier B list), which this review names as the best evidence, a review of nine prospective controlled trials conducted from 1959 to 1978.

Amato et al. (2010), Cochrane review of benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal (ref. 12; on the project's Tier A list, read by another first reader in this round), cited for benzodiazepines as the mainstay and for no single benzodiazepine being superior.

Eyer et al. (2011), Alcohol and Alcoholism: predictors of seizures and delirium tremens in the course of withdrawal (ref. 10; on the project's Tier B list), one of the cited sources of the prevalence and predictor statements.

replication.where_it_stands: A clinical review rather than an evidence synthesis. By its own account the treatment evidence for withdrawal delirium is thin (nine controlled trials from 1959 to 1978 and later uncontrolled studies), and it calls for publicly funded trials. Its descriptive figures should be cited from the primary sources it names (for example Eyer et al., 2011, the 2004 guideline and Amato et al., 2010). Later trials or reviews of treatment for withdrawal delirium were not searched for in this reading, and letters in reply were not searched (no browser in this round).

funding.funder: Not reported (the article has no funding statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest relevant to this article was reported; the author's disclosure forms are available with the full text at NEJM.org and were not read (p. 2113).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, University of California, San Diego, School of Medicine (p. 2109). Three of the 33 references are the author's own: a 2009 Lancet review of alcohol use disorders (ref. 2), a textbook chapter on ethanol and methanol (ref. 5) and the 1995 study of withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens (ref. 17), which supports part of the predictor list. Published in NEJM's Review Article series (editor Dan L. Longo).

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials in patients with DSM-5 withdrawal delirium comparing benzodiazepine-based treatment with alternatives (for example phenobarbital, or dexmedetomidine as an adjunct) on mortality, complications and length of intensive care, together with prospective multicentre cohorts using standardized diagnosis to establish the incidence, case fatality and validated predictors of withdrawal delirium in each care setting.

domains.note: No search strategy, dates or inclusion criteria; a PubMed search for uncontrolled studies after 2004 is mentioned without terms or dates (p. 2111); 33 references chosen by the author (p. 2113).

The evidence base is characterized candidly in general terms (few double-blind trials; the best evidence nine controlled trials from 1959 to 1978; doses approximations from uncontrolled studies; alternatives less well studied; pp. 2111–2112), but no cited study is appraised: the prevalence, case-fatality and predictor figures are given without the designs or settings of their sources, some of which are retrospective by their titles (refs 13 and 16).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Three of 33 references are the author's own (refs 2, 5 and 17), and one of them supports part of the predictor list; the treatment recommendations rest mainly on others' guidelines and reviews (refs 9, 12 and 18 to 22).

The explanation for the lack of trials is hedged, and the Conclusions state that doses are approximations from uncontrolled studies and that data on the best care are lacking; but Table 3 sets out specific regimens as suggested treatment without grading their evidence, the Conclusions name intravenous benzodiazepines as the best treatment without cited comparative evidence, and the statement that alcohol use disorders shorten life by a decade carries no citation (pp. 2109, 2112).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on drug treatment of withdrawal delirium (benzodiazepines against alternatives)
domains.note: The dangers of the alternatives and adjuncts are named (heart block with dexmedetomidine; QT prolongation and seizures with antipsychotics) and they are said to offer few advantages, but the harms of high-dose benzodiazepines are not discussed and the studies of alternatives are cited for amounts, not results. The under-represented side is the evidence on the alternatives and on the harms of the recommended benzodiazepine approach (pp. 2111–2112).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used (model card sc_kish_2017), and the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain (search and selection, high). The review is candid about the thin evidence for treating withdrawal delirium and does not lean on the author's own work, but its selection is unsystematic and its figures are second-hand. It may be cited for the definitions it reproduces (the DSM-5 criteria; the structure and score bands of the CIWA-Ar, attributed to their sources), for the author's characterization of the evidence base (few controlled trials, the best being nine from 1959 to 1978; doses resting on uncontrolled studies) and for what it recommends in general terms, attributed to the author. Figures on incidence, case fatality, timing and predictors should be cited from the primary sources it names; a claim resting only on this review stays at draft (METHODS §5.3).

key_findings.finding: The review states that about 50% of people with an alcohol use disorder have withdrawal symptoms when they cut down or stop drinking and that in 3 to 5% of them grand mal seizures, a delirium or both develop (citing DSM-5); lifetime prevalence of alcohol use disorder in most Western societies is given as 20% of men and 10% of women, and alcohol-related conditions as affecting more than 20% of patients in most medical settings.
key_findings.locator: Opening section (before States of Alcohol Withdrawal), 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures (refs 1 to 3). The statement in the same paragraph that these conditions can shorten life by a decade carries no citation.

key_findings.finding: Alcohol is described as a central nervous system depressant that increases GABA release, with prominent effects at GABA-A receptors, and inhibits NMDA glutamate-receptor activity; with repeated exposure the brain adapts (tolerance), and falling blood alcohol then produces symptoms broadly opposite to the acute effects: insomnia, anxiety, raised pulse, respiration rate, body temperature and blood pressure, and hand tremor. Withdrawal symptoms usually begin within 8 hours after blood alcohol falls, peak at about 72 hours and are markedly reduced by days 5 to 7 of abstinence.
key_findings.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Mild and Moderate Withdrawal, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Cited to reviews and a textbook chapter (refs 4 to 7), not to primary studies.

key_findings.finding: The CIWA-Ar is presented as a clinician-rated 10-item scale (9 items scored 0 to 7, and orientation and clouding of sensorium scored 0 to 4) with totals from 0 to 67: below 8 mild withdrawal that rarely needs medication, 8 to 15 moderate, above 15 severe, with a danger of grand mal seizures, delirium or both; some studies use 10 as the cut-off between mild and moderate. The table is taken from a review by Kosten and O'Connor (ref. 4).
key_findings.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Mild and Moderate Withdrawal, 2nd paragraph (p. 2109, continuing on p. 2110); Table 1 and its footnote (p. 2110)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, pp. 2109–2110 (text; Table 1 checked on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal delirium is defined, following DSM-5, as alcohol withdrawal (stopping or reducing heavy, prolonged drinking, with at least two of eight symptoms: autonomic hyperactivity, hand tremor, insomnia, nausea or vomiting, transient hallucinations or illusions, psychomotor agitation, anxiety, generalized tonic–clonic seizures) together with delirium, a rapid-onset, fluctuating disturbance of attention, awareness and cognition that is a change from normal, without coma or another evolving neurocognitive disorder.
key_findings.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Withdrawal Delirium (Delirium Tremens), 1st paragraph (p. 2110); Table 2 and its footnote (p. 2111)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, pp. 2110–2111 (text read on the rendered pages; Table 2 checked)

key_findings.finding: Prevalence is said to be hard to establish, because clinicians differ in how closely they follow the criteria and rates depend on the setting (outpatient, general medical or psychiatric inpatient, intensive care); most studies estimate that 3 to 5% of patients hospitalized for alcohol withdrawal meet the criteria for withdrawal delirium, and retrospective chart reviews based on general clinicians' diagnoses give higher but less reliable rates.
key_findings.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Withdrawal Delirium (Delirium Tremens), 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand (refs 7, 10 and 11); the settings and periods of these estimates are not given.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, p. 2110 (text read on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Withdrawal delirium usually begins about 3 days after withdrawal symptoms appear and lasts from 1 to 8 days or more, usually 2 or 3 days. About 1 to 4% of hospitalized patients with withdrawal delirium die, a rate the author says could be reduced by timely diagnosis and adequate treatment; death usually results from hyperthermia, cardiac arrhythmias, complications of withdrawal seizures or concomitant medical disorders.
key_findings.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Withdrawal Delirium (Delirium Tremens), 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand: the case-fatality range is cited to four sources (refs 7, 9, 11 and 13) without their settings or periods, and the possible reduction is not quantified.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, p. 2110 (text read on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Predictors of delirium during withdrawal named in the review: CIWA-Ar scores above 15 (especially with systolic blood pressure above 150 mm Hg or pulse above 100 beats per minute), recent withdrawal seizures (seen in 20% of people with delirium), prior withdrawal delirium or seizures, older age, recent misuse of other depressants, and concomitant medical problems, including low potassium or magnesium, low platelet counts, and respiratory, cardiac or gastrointestinal disease.
key_findings.locator: States of Alcohol Withdrawal › Withdrawal Delirium (Delirium Tremens), 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: No effect sizes or designs are given. The sources (refs 7, 10, 11, 13, 16 and 17) include two retrospective studies by their titles (refs 13 and 16) and the author's own 1995 study of 1648 people with alcohol dependence (ref. 17, reference list p. 2113).
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, p. 2110 (text read on the rendered page); reference list p. 2113

key_findings.finding: The author states that few double-blind, controlled, prospective trials of treatment exist, offering the low prevalence of the condition, high treatment costs and a lack of commercial incentive as possible reasons; the best evidence is a 2004 review of nine prospective controlled trials conducted between 1959 and 1978 (Mayo-Smith et al., 2004), together with later uncontrolled studies identified in a PubMed search.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Withdrawal Delirium, 1st paragraph (p. 2110, continuing on p. 2111)
key_findings.note: The PubMed search's terms, dates and selection criteria are not given.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, pp. 2110–2111 (text read on the rendered pages)

key_findings.finding: The review's treatment goals are to control agitation and to lower the risk of seizures, injury and death. It recommends care in a locked inpatient ward or an intensive care unit, because agitation is common and outcomes can be fatal; a physical examination and blood tests to find and treat contributing medical problems; the general supportive care used for any delirium (reorientation, a well-lit room, reassurance, frequent vital-sign checks, adequate hydration); caution with glucose because of the risk of precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy; and care to avoid overhydration in people with alcohol-related cardiac compromise.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Withdrawal Delirium, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 2111); Table 3 (p. 2112)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, pp. 2111–2112 (text; Table 3 checked on the rendered page; its regimens and doses not recorded)

key_findings.finding: The review recommends thiamine and multivitamins, with more thiamine when Wernicke's encephalopathy is suspected, and finds little support for giving magnesium routinely. The amounts it gives are not recorded on this card.

Benzodiazepines are called the mainstay of drug treatment, and no single benzodiazepine has been shown superior to another; Table 3 gives example regimens for a long-acting and a shorter-acting benzodiazepine. The amounts needed vary greatly between patients and can be very large, which the author gives as a reason for treatment in hospital, preferably intensive care, directed by well-trained clinicians. The regimens and doses are not recorded on this card.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Withdrawal Delirium, 4th paragraph (p. 2111); Table 3 (p. 2112)
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, pp. 2111–2112 (text; Table 3 checked on the rendered page; its regimens and doses not recorded)

key_findings.finding: Phenobarbital, clomethiazole, midazolam, carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine have been proposed for uncomplicated withdrawal, but data on their use in withdrawal delirium are lacking. Propofol (especially in intubated patients) and dexmedetomidine (an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist used in intensive care; not usable with heart block, and requiring close monitoring of blood pressure and heart rate) are named for patients who do not respond to high benzodiazepine doses. None of these has been studied as well as benzodiazepines, and each is said to carry additional dangers and few advantages for most patients. Haloperidol is listed as an adjunct for severe agitation or hallucinosis, with the warning that antipsychotics can prolong the QT interval and make seizures more likely.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Withdrawal Delirium, 5th paragraph (p. 2111, continuing on p. 2112) and 6th paragraph (p. 2112); Table 3 (p. 2112)
key_findings.note: Cited to reviews and small or uncontrolled studies (refs 7, 13, 20 to 22 and 25 to 33); no results of these studies are given in the review.
key_findings.source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf, pp. 2111–2112 (text read on the rendered pages)

key_findings.finding: The Conclusions call withdrawal delirium an uncommon, serious complication of withdrawal that is best treated with intravenous benzodiazepines; they state that all doses described in the review are approximations based on uncontrolled studies and that data on the most effective care are lacking, and call for treatment trials sponsored by the National Institutes of Health because the low profit potential may deter pharmaceutical companies.

reporting_issues.issue: The same 3 to 5% range is given for two different quantities: on p. 2109 for grand mal seizures, delirium or both among people with an alcohol use disorder who have withdrawal symptoms (citing DSM-5), and on p. 2110 for withdrawal delirium among patients hospitalized for alcohol withdrawal (refs 7, 10 and 11).
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominators (everyone with withdrawal symptoms against hospitalized patients) and the outcomes (seizures or delirium against delirium) differ; a claim must keep them apart and should cite the primary sources.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that alcohol use disorders can shorten life by a decade carries no citation; the reference markers in that paragraph belong to the sentences before and after it.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not citable from this review; a claim about life expectancy needs a primary source.

reporting_issues.issue: The CIWA-Ar description and its score bands are cited to two secondary sources (refs 4 and 8; the table to the review by Kosten and O'Connor, ref. 4), and the scale's development paper (Sullivan et al., on the project's Tier B list) is not cited.
reporting_issues.consequence: Score bands used in claims should be checked against the instrument's original paper rather than taken from this review.
